A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PFedRL-Rep research work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: Sections 4.3 and 5 and Appendix G report original CliffWalking, CartPole, Acrobot, and Hopper experiments, including learning curves, runtime comparisons, and personalization analyses.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, with additional computation–personalization and environment-discrepancy results in Appendix G.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–4 retain the same personalized weight updates, shared representation updates, and server averaging. The TD, Q-learning, DQN, and Hopper DDPG instantiations already appear in v1; v2 does not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: The benchmark families remain CliffWalking, CartPole, Acrobot, and Hopper. Appendix G.4 adds a scenario sweeping inter-agent length discrepancy from identical environments to a maximum discrepancy of 0.04, extending the tested heterogeneity conditions.

E2.justification: The standalone speedup comparison changes: v1 explicitly compares convergence against a non-personalized counterpart, whereas v2 Figure 11 reports only PFedDQN-Rep convergence times. The retained benchmark comparisons keep their baseline sets, and new Figures 12–13 reuse existing baselines.

E3.justification: Figure 11 changes from relative speedup for CartPole and Acrobot to absolute CartPole convergence times; G.2 specifies duplicating two environments for N = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. New G.3–G.4 introduce worst-agent expected squared value-estimation error and agent-count/discrepancy sweeps. These substantially extend the evaluation design, while Table 2 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained personalization heatmaps, v2 adds quantitative analyses of computation versus worst-agent personalization error (Figure 12) and sensitivity to environment discrepancy (Figure 13). It also revises the speedup validation. These address tradeoff and robustness questions that v1 did not quantify.

E5.justification: Tables 3–4 retain the same mean, variance, and median reporting. Neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Renaming the statistical-results discussion does not change its statistical methodology.

E6.justification: New Figures 12–13 report a favorable computation–personalization tradeoff and less deterioration with increasing discrepancy than PerDQNAvg and FedAsynQ-ImAvg. Figure 11 replaces the earlier two-environment speedup results with absolute CartPole timings. These are new or replaced findings, not comparable-setting performance gains; Tables 3–4 and the original learning curves remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (56) newly defines personalization quality through the maximum expected squared value-estimation error across agents. The convergence assumptions, Theorem 4.13, Corollary 4.15, and their proofs retain their mathematical substance; swapping the names C1 and C2 in Equation (16) is equivalent notation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the shared-representation personalization framework, the claimed first linear speedup for the stated TD setting under Markovian noise, and improved heterogeneous-environment learning and generalization. The appendix additions support these contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: G.2 explains why environment-dependent constants should remain fixed when varying agent count and acknowledges runtime overhead. G.3–G.4 add interpretations of worst-agent error, computational tradeoffs, and degradation under increasing heterogeneity. The limitation that the convergence analysis does not cover control remains.

D1.justification: G.2 newly specifies the speedup experiment's base pole lengths, 0.36 and 0.42, and replication scheme; G.4 describes the discrepancy sweep. Architecture, hyperparameters, and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. Reproduction of G.4 remains ambiguous because its Hopper description uses pole terminology and DQN method names.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to federated RL, personalized learning, representation learning, and two-timescale stochastic approximation are retained. Related-work and comparison passages are edited without adding literature or changing the novelty position.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits the abstract, theoretical remarks, proof explanations, and control discussion. Appendix G gains numbered subsections, and acknowledgements, conference headers, and an affiliation update are added. The overall narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces Figure 11, adds Figures 12–13, enlarges the Hopper display, and relocates retained figures and tables. v1 Figures 12–14 correspond to v2 Figures 16, 14, and 15. These are localized display additions and layout changes; most existing visual content is preserved.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the speedup evaluation more interpretable through explicit environment replication and adds useful quantitative evidence about personalization costs and heterogeneity sensitivity. The improvement is limited: the central theory and established benchmark results are unchanged, speedup evidence is narrowed to CartPole, and G.4 leaves its environment/method configuration ambiguous.
